title: Dwarf Dreadnought
subheader: Steam-powered ironclad Man O' War and apex warship of the Dwarf Navy
description:
## Overview

The **Dwarf Dreadnought**, also known as the **Grudgebreaker-class Battleship**, is regarded as the greatest steam-powered ironclad in the Dwarf Navy, and by some captains as the most powerful ship afloat. Though derived from earlier ironclad Man O' War designs, a dreadnought surpasses them in nearly every measure: heavier gun decks, thicker armor, greater speed under steam, and a still-sizeable crew complement.

## Propulsion and Mobility

Dreadnoughts are built around a distinctive propulsion system: linked boiler arrays drive **twin side paddle wheels** as well as a **single oversized stern wheel**. This arrangement gives exceptional thrust for such a massive hull and makes the vessel notoriously hard to immobilize.

Because power is split across side and rear paddle locations, a dreadnought can continue moving even after one drive section is disabled. Only destruction of both paddle systems will halt it completely. With side paddles intact, it can also pivot on the spot like other steam or oared warships; without them, it handles more like a sailing vessel and turns far less sharply.

## Armament and Armor

The class is famous for its extraordinary firepower. Contemporary accounts claim a single dreadnought can carry more guns than a squadron of monitors, with steam-powered swivel mountings that bring batteries to bear forward, aft, and broadside.

Its ironclad protection is equally formidable: hull plating can exceed a foot in thickness, allowing the ship to absorb punishment that would cripple lighter warships. Combined with all-arc gunnery, this durability makes dreadnoughts central to Dwarf naval doctrine.

## Operational Reputation

Mariner lore repeatedly cites dreadnought actions in the **Black Gulf** and off **Sartosa**, where entire pirate fleets were allegedly broken by these iron leviathans. While such reports are often embellished, they reflect the class's strategic reputation as a fleet-anchor and terror to raiders.

## Cultural and Historical Context

Dwarfs traditionally favored mountain holds over open water and had little interest in sail-and-oar seamanship, which they often viewed as elven practice. Large-scale steam engineering transformed this outlook. By making iron float and engines independent of wind or tide, Dwarf shipwrights claimed they had imposed the mastery of earth over water—and outdone elven mariners by craft and industry.

Only a limited number of Dwarf ironclads exist, and each vessel is effectively bespoke. Even among them, the dreadnought stands apart as the peak expression of Dwarf naval engineering and grudgebound firepower.
